subtopic_detail: Progressive difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids with a normal endoscopy
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 46 year old woman with two years of food sticking in the chest. She says liquids have been just as difficult as solids from the beginning and that she often has to stand up and stretch her neck to make things go down.

She regurgitates undigested food onto her pillow at night and has lost 6 kg. She was treated with a proton pump inhibitor for eighteen months for presumed reflux without benefit. Upper endoscopy performed last month was reported as normal to the level of the stomach, with no stricture, no ring, no oesophagitis and no mucosal abnormality, and biopsies taken from the proximal and distal oesophagus showed no eosinophilic infiltrate. She has never lived outside Australia and takes no other medication.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg per square metre, no cervical lymphadenopathy, chest clear, abdomen soft with no mass
data_table.Investigations: Upper endoscopy normal with no stricture or mucosal lesion, oesophageal biopsies with no eosinophilic infiltrate, haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-155), C-reactive protein 2 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: High resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise peristalsis and relaxation of the lower sphincter
options.rationale: Dysphagia to liquids and solids equally from the outset, with regurgitation of undigested food and failure of acid suppression, indicates a motility disorder rather than a structural one, and endoscopy has already excluded mechanical obstruction. Manometry is the diagnostic standard and also subtypes the disorder, which determines whether pneumatic dilatation, myotomy or a peroral endoscopic approach is chosen. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

options.text: Repeat upper endoscopy with careful retroflexed views and further biopsies of the distal oesophagus
options.rationale: A normal endoscopy with negative biopsies has already answered the structural and eosinophilic questions, and repeating it is unlikely to reveal a motility abnormality that endoscopy cannot assess. It is worth repeating only if the first study was technically limited or symptoms change. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

options.text: Twenty four hour ambulatory oesophageal pH monitoring to quantify acid exposure and symptom correlation
options.rationale: Ambulatory pH testing evaluates reflux disease and is useful when symptoms persist despite acid suppression and the diagnosis of reflux is in doubt. Regurgitation of undigested food rather than acid, with equal difficulty for liquids, points away from reflux as the mechanism. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

options.text: Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen to look for a malignancy infiltrating the gastric cardia
options.rationale: A tumour at the cardia can imitate this picture and is the classic pseudo presentation, which is exactly why endoscopy comes first and has been normal here. Cross sectional imaging is added when the history is short, the weight loss is rapid, or manometry findings are combined with an older patient. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

options.text: Videofluoroscopic swallow assessment with a speech pathologist to evaluate the oropharyngeal phase
options.rationale: Videofluoroscopy assesses oropharyngeal swallowing and is used when there is coughing at the start of a swallow, nasal regurgitation or a neurological cause. This woman localises the problem to the chest and initiates swallows normally. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

explanation.summary: The first branch point in dysphagia is whether difficulty is for solids alone, which suggests a mechanical narrowing, or for solids and liquids equally, which suggests a motility disorder. Achalasia is the archetype of the latter and is caused by loss of inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus, producing failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and absent peristalsis. It typically presents in the fourth to sixth decades with slowly progressive dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, nocturnal cough, weight loss and years of ineffective reflux treatment. Endoscopy is performed first, principally to exclude a tumour at the cardia that can mimic the manometric picture, and barium swallow may show the tapered distal narrowing, but high resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and identifies the subtype that guides treatment. Options include pneumatic dilatation, laparoscopic myotomy with fundoplication, peroral endoscopic myotomy, and botulinum toxin injection for those unfit for definitive treatment.
key_points: Equal difficulty with liquids and solids from the start indicates a motility disorder
Endoscopy comes first to exclude a tumour at the cardia mimicking achalasia
High resolution manometry is the diagnostic standard and defines the subtype
Years of ineffective proton pump inhibitor therapy is a characteristic history
Treatment options are dilatation, myotomy, peroral endoscopic myotomy or botulinum toxin
explanation.pearls: Suspect a malignancy at the cardia rather than primary achalasia when the history is shorter than six months, weight loss is disproportionate, or the patient is over sixty, because tumour infiltration of the myenteric plexus reproduces the manometric findings exactly and cross sectional imaging or endoscopic ultrasound is then required before any dilatation is attempted.

subtopic_detail: Food impaction requiring endoscopic disimpaction in a young man with atopy
stem:
You are the gastroenterology registrar attending a 23 year old man who presented last night unable to swallow his own saliva after eating steak. The impacted bolus has just been removed endoscopically and he is comfortable in recovery.

He tells you he has been cutting food into small pieces and drinking water with every mouthful for the past three years, and that this is his second impaction. He has asthma treated with an inhaled corticosteroid, hay fever and a childhood history of eczema. At endoscopy the operator described concentric rings along the oesophagus with linear furrows and scattered white exudate, and no stricture or ulceration. He has taken a proton pump inhibitor intermittently for what he was told was reflux, with no clear benefit.

data_table.Examination: Comfortable in recovery, chest clear, no surgical emphysema in the neck, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Endoscopy showing concentric oesophageal rings, linear furrows and white exudate with no stricture or ulceration, bolus removed intact, eosinophil count 0.7 x10^9/L (less than 0.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange high resolution oesophageal manometry to exclude a primary disorder of oesophageal motility
options.rationale: Manometry is the correct test for dysphagia to solids and liquids equally with a normal endoscopy, and abnormal motility can coexist here. It does not establish the diagnosis when the endoscopic appearance already points to a mucosal inflammatory disease that biopsy can confirm. (Source: GESA: Oesophageal disorders)

options.text: Take multiple oesophageal biopsies from proximal and distal sites and count eosinophils per high power field
options.rationale: Rings, furrows and exudate in a young atopic man with recurrent impaction is the endoscopic signature of eosinophilic oesophagitis, but the diagnosis is histological and requires at least six biopsies from two levels because the infiltrate is patchy. Confirming it changes management to topical corticosteroid, dietary elimination or a proton pump inhibitor trial with a defined histological endpoint. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Arrange serum specific immunoglobulin E testing to a broad food panel and eliminate every positive food
options.rationale: Specific immunoglobulin E and skin prick testing correlate poorly with the foods that actually drive this disease, which is not classically immunoglobulin E mediated. Elimination guided by panel testing produces unnecessarily restricted diets without reliable histological remission. (Source: ASCIA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Arrange endoscopic dilatation at a second procedure to widen the oesophagus and prevent further impaction
options.rationale: Dilatation relieves fibrostenotic narrowing and has a role in established strictures, but the endoscopist reported no stricture and dilatation does not treat the underlying inflammation. Dilating before controlling inflammation also carries a higher risk of mucosal tearing. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

options.text: Increase the dose of his inhaled corticosteroid on the basis that his asthma control is driving symptoms
options.rationale: Asthma and this oesophageal condition share an atopic background but inhaled therapy delivered to the airway does not treat oesophageal inflammation. The formulations used for the oesophagus are deliberately designed to be swallowed and to coat the mucosa. (Source: GESA: Eosinophilic oesophagitis)

explanation.summary: Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a chronic immune mediated disease that has become the leading cause of food impaction in young adults, typically men with a background of asthma, allergic rhinitis or eczema. Patients often normalise years of adaptive behaviour such as prolonged chewing, cutting food finely, drinking with every mouthful and avoiding meat and bread, so the history must be sought directly. Endoscopy shows concentric rings, linear furrows, white exudate, oedema and sometimes a narrow calibre oesophagus, but appearances can be normal, so the diagnosis rests on histology with at least six biopsies from two oesophageal levels and a threshold of fifteen eosinophils per high power field. Treatment options are a proton pump inhibitor trial, swallowed topical corticosteroid formulated to coat the mucosa, and dietary elimination, each assessed by repeat biopsy rather than by symptoms alone. Dilatation addresses established fibrostenotic narrowing but does not treat the inflammation.
key_points: Recurrent food impaction in a young atopic adult should prompt this diagnosis
At least six biopsies from two levels are required because the infiltrate is patchy
Fifteen eosinophils per high power field is the histological threshold
Adaptive eating behaviours conceal years of symptoms unless asked about directly
Response is assessed histologically because symptoms improve ahead of inflammation
explanation.pearls: Ask directly how long a meal takes and whether the patient avoids steak, bread and rice, because these adaptive behaviours are the most sensitive historical clue and patients almost never volunteer them, having assumed for years that everyone eats that way.

subtopic_detail: Unilateral facial weakness including the forehead developing over a day
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 41 year old man who woke twenty hours ago unable to close his right eye and with the right side of his mouth drooping. He is frightened that he has had a stroke.

He describes an ache behind the right ear that began the day before the weakness, and says sounds seem uncomfortably loud on that side. On examination he cannot raise the right eyebrow or wrinkle the right forehead, cannot bury the right eyelashes, and the right nasolabial fold is flattened. Eye movements are full, pupils are equal and reactive, there is no limb weakness, no sensory loss and no ataxia, and speech is clear with normal tongue and palatal movement. There is no vesicular rash in or around the ear or on the palate, and the tympanic membranes are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, BP 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Complete right sided facial weakness including frontalis, incomplete eye closure with Bell phenomenon, hyperacusis on the right, normal extraocular movements, no limb or sensory deficit, no rash in the ear canal or on the palate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Referral for facial nerve electrophysiological studies within the next week to establish the prognosis
options.rationale: Electrophysiology has a prognostic role in complete palsy but is generally performed after the first week once degeneration would be detectable, and it does not alter the immediate decision to treat. Delaying the corticosteroid to obtain it would waste the treatment window. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Reassurance with facial exercises and review in two weeks if the weakness has not begun to improve
options.rationale: Most patients do recover spontaneously, which is why this advice feels safe, but a corticosteroid given within the first three days meaningfully increases the proportion achieving complete recovery. Watching and waiting also leaves an unprotected cornea exposed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Oral prednisolone started today with lubricating eye drops and an eye pad for overnight protection
options.rationale: Involvement of the forehead localises the lesion to the lower motor neuron, and a corticosteroid started within seventy two hours of onset significantly improves the chance of complete recovery. Eye protection is equally important because incomplete closure with reduced blinking risks exposure keratopathy and corneal ulceration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Urgent computed tomography of the brain with consideration of thrombolysis for an acute stroke syndrome
options.rationale: A stroke affecting the facial nerve nucleus or its supranuclear supply spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical innervation to the upper face, and it is usually accompanied by limb or speech findings. Complete forehead involvement with no other deficit points to a peripheral lesion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Oral valaciclovir alone for seven days on the basis of probable herpes simplex reactivation in the nerve
options.rationale: Antiviral therapy alone is inferior to corticosteroid and is not recommended as monotherapy in this condition. Adding an antiviral to a corticosteroid is considered in severe or complete palsy, but it never replaces the steroid. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic facial nerve palsy is diagnosed clinically and the single most important examination step is to test the forehead, since sparing of frontalis indicates an upper motor neuron lesion requiring urgent stroke assessment while involvement of the forehead localises to the nerve itself. Associated features that support a peripheral lesion include postauricular pain, hyperacusis from stapedius involvement, and altered taste on the anterior tongue. A corticosteroid started within seventy two hours of onset improves the rate of complete recovery, and the evidence for adding an antiviral is weaker but it is often given alongside in severe or complete palsy. Eye care is essential and must be prescribed explicitly, since incomplete closure with a reduced blink reflex causes exposure keratopathy. Ramsay Hunt syndrome must be excluded by inspecting the external ear canal, pinna and palate for vesicles, because it requires antiviral therapy and carries a worse prognosis.
key_points: Forehead involvement separates a lower motor neuron lesion from a stroke
Corticosteroid within seventy two hours improves the rate of complete recovery
Antiviral monotherapy is inferior and is never used in place of the steroid
Prescribe lubricant and overnight eye protection to prevent exposure keratopathy
Inspect the ear canal and palate for vesicles indicating Ramsay Hunt syndrome
explanation.pearls: Review any patient whose facial weakness fails to show some recovery by three months, because the diagnosis of idiopathic palsy assumes improvement begins within weeks, and a slowly progressive or non recovering facial weakness demands imaging of the nerve along its whole course to exclude a parotid malignancy or a schwannoma.

subtopic_detail: Brief positional spinning on rolling over in bed with a normal neurological examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 64 year old woman with four days of spinning that comes on when she rolls over in bed or tips her head back to hang washing. Each episode lasts under a minute and settles if she keeps still.

She is completely well between episodes and has no symptoms while sitting still. She has no hearing loss, no tinnitus, no ear fullness and no headache. Neurological examination shows normal eye movements with no gaze evoked nystagmus, normal finger nose and heel shin testing, normal gait with a negative Romberg test, and intact cranial nerves. There is no spontaneous nystagmus when she looks straight ahead. Her blood pressure shows no postural drop and her heart rhythm is regular.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min regular, BP 134/80 mmHg lying and 130/78 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No spontaneous nystagmus, full smooth pursuit without gaze evoked nystagmus, normal coordination and gait, negative Romberg, hearing normal to whispered voice bilaterally, tympanic membranes normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and posterior fossa to exclude a central cause of vertigo
options.rationale: Imaging is directed at features suggesting a central lesion such as gaze evoked or direction changing nystagmus, ataxia out of proportion to the vertigo, other cranial nerve signs, or new headache. None of those are present and imaging without them has a very low yield. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start betahistine and a low salt diet with a trial of fluid restriction to reduce endolymphatic pressure
options.rationale: This regimen targets Meniere disease, which produces attacks lasting twenty minutes to several hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. Her episodes are far shorter and her hearing is entirely normal. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Refer for formal vestibular rehabilitation therapy as the initial management of her positional symptoms
options.rationale: Vestibular rehabilitation is valuable for incomplete central compensation after vestibular neuritis and for residual unsteadiness once repositioning has succeeded. It is slower and less effective than a repositioning manoeuvre for canal debris and should not displace it as first treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Perform the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre and proceed to a repositioning manoeuvre if it is positive
options.rationale: Episodes lasting under a minute triggered by head position change, with no symptoms between attacks and a normal neurological and otological examination, is positional vertigo of the posterior semicircular canal, and the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre reproduces it with a characteristic latency and fatigable upbeating torsional nystagmus. A positive result is treated immediately with the Epley repositioning manoeuvre, which resolves symptoms in the majority after one or two attempts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Prescribe prochlorperazine regularly for two weeks to suppress the vestibular symptoms she describes
options.rationale: Vestibular sedatives are for the continuous vertigo and vomiting of acute vestibular neuritis over a few days, and they impair central compensation when continued. They also do nothing to move the displaced otoconia that generate positional symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Vertigo is best sorted by timing and triggers rather than by the quality of the sensation. Brief episodes lasting seconds to a minute provoked by head position change indicate benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, attacks of twenty minutes to hours with fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus indicate Meniere disease, and a single prolonged episode lasting days with continuous vertigo indicates vestibular neuritis or, if there are central signs, a posterior circulation stroke. The Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre both confirms posterior canal involvement and identifies the affected side, with nystagmus that has a brief latency, lasts under a minute and fatigues on repetition. The Epley repositioning manoeuvre is the treatment and is effective in most patients within one or two attempts. Vestibular sedatives are reserved for short term symptom control in acute continuous vertigo, since they hinder the central compensation that recovery depends on.
key_points: Timing and trigger separate positional vertigo from Meniere disease and neuritis
Dix-Hallpike confirms the diagnosis and identifies the affected side
Latency, duration under a minute and fatigability characterise peripheral nystagmus
Epley repositioning is the treatment and works in most patients quickly
Vestibular sedatives impair compensation and are not used for positional vertigo
explanation.pearls: Treat direction changing or gaze evoked nystagmus, nystagmus without latency that does not fatigue, or truncal ataxia so severe the patient cannot sit unsupported as central until proven otherwise, since a cerebellar infarct can present with isolated vertigo and a superficially reassuring examination.

subtopic_detail: Acute monoarthritis of the knee in an older patient with chondrocalcinosis on radiograph
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 76 year old woman with a hot swollen left knee that came on over twelve hours. She has been admitted for four days with a community acquired pneumonia and has been improving on antibiotics.

She has osteoarthritis of both knees and takes no regular anti inflammatory medication. She has never had gout and has no tophi. The knee is warm, swollen with a tense effusion and painful through the last thirty degrees of flexion. There is no break in the skin over the joint, no cellulitis and no ulceration. A radiograph of the knee shows linear calcification within the meniscal cartilage of both knees. She is on no diuretic and her renal function has been stable throughout the admission.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Warm swollen left knee with tense effusion, restricted terminal flexion, intact overlying skin with no cellulitis, no tophi, other joints unaffected
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 13.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5), serum urate 0.34 mmol/L (0.15-0.45), creatinine 78 micromol/L (45-90), knee radiograph showing linear meniscal calcification bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral colchicine on the basis that the cartilage calcification confirms a crystal induced arthritis
options.rationale: Cartilage calcification is a radiological finding that is common in older people and indicates crystal deposition, not that crystals are causing this particular attack. Treating without aspiration risks missing a septic joint, which destroys cartilage within days. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Start intravenous flucloxacillin empirically for septic arthritis and arrange orthopaedic review tomorrow
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are correct once the joint has been sampled, but giving them before aspiration reduces the yield of synovial culture and can leave the diagnosis permanently uncertain. Aspiration is quick and should precede the first dose whenever it does not delay treatment of a septic patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence allopurinol at low dose with colchicine cover and titrate to a target serum urate concentration
options.rationale: Urate lowering therapy treats gout and is never started during an acute attack without cover, and her serum urate is within the reference range. The radiographic calcification also points to a different crystal species altogether. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee to assess for osteomyelitis of the distal femur or tibia
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is useful when osteomyelitis is suspected or when the source of infection is unclear after aspiration. It is slower, less available and answers a narrower question than synovial fluid analysis in an acutely swollen joint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Aspirate the joint and send fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture and polarised light microscopy
options.rationale: Any acutely inflamed joint requires aspiration before treatment because septic arthritis and crystal arthritis are clinically indistinguishable and can coexist, and this woman has a concurrent infection and a fever. Polarised microscopy separates the positively birefringent rhomboid crystals of calcium pyrophosphate from the negatively birefringent needles of urate, while culture answers the question that matters most. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease is common in older adults and its acute attacks most often affect the knee or wrist, frequently triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery or trauma. Chondrocalcinosis on radiograph, seen as linear calcification within fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage, supports the diagnosis but is a chronic finding present in many asymptomatic older people, so it can never establish the cause of a particular attack. Septic arthritis remains the diagnosis that must not be missed, is clinically indistinguishable at the bedside, and can coexist with crystal arthritis in the same joint, so aspiration for cell count, Gram stain, culture and polarised microscopy precedes treatment. Under polarised light the crystals of calcium pyrophosphate are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent, in contrast to the strongly negatively birefringent needles of monosodium urate. Once infection is excluded, treatment is with a non steroidal anti inflammatory, colchicine, or intra articular or systemic corticosteroid according to comorbidity.
key_points: Chondrocalcinosis is a chronic radiological finding and never proves the cause of an attack
Septic arthritis is indistinguishable clinically and can coexist with crystal disease
Aspirate before antibiotics wherever this does not delay treating a septic patient
Rhomboid positively birefringent crystals indicate calcium pyrophosphate deposition
Attacks are often triggered by intercurrent illness, surgery or trauma
explanation.pearls: Investigate for an underlying metabolic cause when calcium pyrophosphate disease presents before the age of sixty or affects multiple joints, because haemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesaemia and hypophosphatasia all predispose to it and identifying one changes management well beyond the joint.
